data.description: Generate retrospective.md as required plan output to capture what assumptions were wrong, where adaptation occurred, and feed learning back into future planning prompts for continuous improvement

data.note: Core concept: retrospective.md as a required plan output that captures learning from execution
Key questions retrospective should answer: wrong assumptions, adaptation points, specification quality (over/under), patterns for future plans
Critical insight: retrospectives feed future planning prompts automatically - structured reflection instead of memory
This creates continuous improvement for LLM collaboration - plans get better over time through learning loop

data.content:
Retrospective should be generated at the end, right after executing the plan. Not after every milestone or on-demand, but as part of the process. RiotPlan does this with a prompt that tells whatever is running the plan to do a retrospective, incorporating all execution data.

After executing every step, there should be a summary written about that step that includes self-reflection about executing that step. The status file should have those step reflections.

There should be an overall retrospective.md file in the plan once it's done (separate from step reflections). Don't want a repository of retrospectives - they should just be part of the plan format.

On influencing future plans: when creating a new plan, I can point it at other plans and say "learn from that plan."

Structure should be more freeform, not fixed schema. Want a retrospective for each step, plus the overall retrospective.

Driving force: have run about 100 plans, want the system to give feedback on what I can do differently or what the system can do differently to make it easier to explore ideas, create plans, execute plans. Almost everything with reasoning agents involves asking them to look back and understand what could have been done differently.

data.note: Timing: retrospective generated at end of plan execution, as part of the process (not on-demand or per-milestone)
Two-level reflection: (1) step-level self-reflection after each step execution, stored in STATUS.md (2) overall retrospective.md at plan completion
Retrospectives are part of plan format, not a separate repository - they live with the plan
Learning mechanism: when creating new plan, can point at other plans to learn from them (explicit reference, not automatic)
Structure: freeform, not fixed schema - allows natural reflection rather than checkbox compliance
Motivation: after 100+ plans, need feedback mechanism to improve both user behavior and system behavior
Pattern: reasoning agents work best when they look back and understand what could have been done differently

data.question: How does STATUS.md get updated? Currently seems to replace rather than append - need clarity on whether step reflections should append or be structured sections

data.content:
Step reflections: Written by agent after step completes. Agent should have memory of what it just did. Should capture: time taken, deviations, surprises, blockers, AND enumerate what could have been done differently to make it more straightforward.

Step reflections MUST be visible to subsequent steps - step 5 should learn from step 3's reflection. This creates a communication mechanism between steps.

Overall retrospective.md: Should incorporate/synthesize all the step summaries. Should compare original plan (what we thought we'd do) vs what actually happened.

Not a summary - we already have summary.md and status.md. This is different: high-value feedback focused on what went right, what went wrong, and what could have been done differently in the plan. Designed for: "if I'm going to create another plan like this in the future, what could I have done differently?" Want it to be very creative.

Learning from other plans: During idea exploration, might say "what I'm doing here is related to what we did over there, can you consider the retrospective from that plan?" This helps inform questions that will be asked. Don't automatically detect related plans - RiotPlan doesn't have an index yet.

Format: Human-readable prose, possibly with YAML front matter. In fact, many files (step status, plan status, etc.) probably need YAML front matter.

data.content:
When executing a step, agent should receive the previous status and previous reflection content from earlier steps. Likes the proposed STATUS.md structure with step sections.

Triggering retrospectives: Yes to all three - a command like riotplan_generate_retrospective, automatic when last step completes, and part of plan complete workflow. All of these.

Referencing other retrospectives: Read the retrospective file and include it in context. Not through riotplan_idea_add_evidence. But it should be wrapped in a way that informs WHY it's being included.

YAML front matter is a separate concern from retrospectives.

data.content:
Had other instances of asking reasoning models to do self-reflection. In another project that does commit messages, there's a "do self-reflection" but it's really not doing inference - just code that says "if this, then write this." That's NOT what I want here.

For self-reflection, I'm looking for a genuinely good model to do a review of what happened. Not something simple, predictable, or full of rote responses. This self-reflection feature is where we start to see LLMs and reasoning models astound us with creative ideas we haven't thought through yet.

When turning this into a plan, think about HOW we execute this. It shouldn't be a set of if-statements or templated responses. This needs real reasoning.
data.context: User emphasizing that reflection must leverage real model reasoning, not templated logic
data.speaker: user

data.note: Anti-pattern: templated/rote self-reflection ("if X then write Y"). Have seen this fail in commit message tools - produces predictable, low-value output
Self-reflection must use genuine model reasoning - this is where LLMs should astound with creative insights we haven't considered

data.constraint: Reflections must be generated by real model inference, not templated logic or if-statement heuristics
Prompt design for reflections must encourage creative, surprising, high-value insights - not checkbox compliance

data.content:
When running plans now, adding own instructions before going from idea to plan. Telling it "here are the models available" - typically Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5 - and saying "choose one of those three models for each step."

For self-reflection, maybe everything stops and gives you time to switch to a very high-powered model. Could see using Opus 4.6 for the self-reflection. Retrospectives demand probably the highest level of model available.

This relates to a broader concept: multi-model execution. Currently creating plans with Opus 4.6, then stepping down to Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus for plan execution. Multi-model execution is probably a whole separate plan.

But specifically for retrospectives: they need the best model available. The creative, surprising insights come from the most capable reasoning.

data.content:
Wants two blog posts as part of this plan:

1. The Natural Model Tier Map - about creating plans with a different (higher) model than you execute them with, then running retrospectives with an even more powerful model. The tiered model workflow.

2. Self-Reflection in LLM Collaboration - about how self-reflection works, why it's important to get right, why it needs real reasoning (not templated responses), and the difference between rote reflection and genuine creative insight from a capable model.

data.name: Integrated State Approach
data.description: Add reflection as a first-class field in the step state model and the plan completion workflow. When step_complete is called, the agent passes a reflection string that gets persisted in plan state. Since STATUS.md is regenerated each time, reflections survive regeneration because they're in the underlying data model. A new 'Reflections' section appears in STATUS.md under each step. The execute_step prompt is updated to read STATUS.md (which includes prior reflections) before starting work. At plan completion, a new riotplan_step_complete call on the final step triggers retrospective generation — a new MCP tool (riotplan_generate_retrospective) reads all step reflections + the original plan + execution data and generates retrospective.md using a carefully crafted prompt designed for genuine model reasoning. The two blog posts are deliverables written as part of the plan. The retrospective prompt is the crown jewel — it must invite creative, surprising analysis, not templated output.
tradeoffs: + Reflections are durable — survive STATUS.md regeneration because they're in the data model
+ Clean integration — step_complete already exists, just needs a reflection parameter
+ STATUS.md becomes the single source of truth for execution state AND reflection
+ Natural workflow — reflection happens right when the agent has full memory of what it just did
- Requires schema change to step state model (migration concern for existing plans)
- step_complete becomes a bigger operation (reflection text can be long)
- STATUS.md grows significantly with reflections included — could become noisy for quick status checks
- Tighter coupling between status tracking and reflection
assumptions: Existing plans without reflections can be handled gracefully (reflection field is optional)
The agent executing steps has enough context to write meaningful reflections at step_complete time
STATUS.md regeneration is the right place to surface reflections to subsequent steps

data.name: Layered Reflection Approach
data.description: Keep step state and STATUS.md focused on execution tracking. Add reflection as a separate layer with its own files and tools. After step_complete, a new tool riotplan_step_reflect writes a reflection file to a reflections/ directory (e.g., reflections/01-reflection.md). The execute_step prompt is updated to read both the step file AND any prior reflection files before starting work. STATUS.md gets a lightweight 'Reflection' column (just a checkmark showing reflection exists) but the full content lives in separate files. At plan completion, riotplan_generate_retrospective reads all reflection files + plan data and generates retrospective.md. The reflection files are freeform prose — no schema, just the agent's genuine analysis. The retrospective prompt is designed to synthesize these into creative, high-value feedback. Blog posts are deliverables. The retrospective tool signals that a high-tier model should be used.
tradeoffs: + Clean separation of concerns — status tracking vs reflection are different jobs
+ Reflection files can be rich and detailed without bloating STATUS.md
+ No schema migration — step state model stays as-is, new files are additive
+ Each reflection is a standalone document that can be read independently
+ Easier to reference individual step reflections from future plans
- Two-tool workflow per step (step_complete + step_reflect) instead of one
- Reflection could be forgotten if agent doesn't call the second tool
- More files in the plan directory (reflections/ adds per-step files)
- Need to ensure execute_step prompt reads reflection files (extra context loading)
assumptions: Agents will reliably call step_reflect after step_complete if the prompt instructs them to
Separate reflection files are better than embedded reflections for readability
The extra file I/O per step is acceptable overhead

data.reason: Clean separation of concerns, freeform standalone reflection files are better for rich prose and cross-plan referencing, avoids schema migration, STATUS.md stays focused on execution tracking. Two-tool risk is manageable through prompt design.
